question: European Citizens’ Initiative ECI(2024)0000081 calls for measures to transition to plantbased agriculture, in the interests of animal welfare, environmental protection and health. The validation of signatures, based on the certificates from Member States uploaded in the file exchange service, resulted in a very significant discrepancy between the number of signatures collected and the number of valid signatures2. 1.
What specific factors were the main causes of this very high number of invalid signatures3?

What measures does the Commission intend to take to ensure that either fewer signatures are declared invalid or fewer invalid signatures are submitted, and what measures are available to re-examine the signatures declared invalid with regard to their validation?
To what extent will the Commission address the substance of the citizens’ initiative despite the high number of invalid signatures?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (15.9.2026) The European citizens’ initiative (ECI) ‘Stop Cruelty Stop Slaughter’ collected statements of support from 24 September 2024 to 24 September 2025.

In accordance with Article 12(2) of Regulation (EU) 2019/788 (ECI Regulation)1, on 20 November 2025, the initiative organisers submitted the statements of support to the Member State authorities responsible for verifying and certifying statements of support from their nationals. The verification process ended on 19 February 2026.

The Commission’s online collection system applies automated checks to reduce incorrectly completed statements of support. These include checks on whether required data have been entered in the prescribed format and warnings where the data entered appear to duplicate an earlier statement of support. The verification of the statements of support is the sole responsibility of Member States.

They complete the verification ‘on the basis of appropriate checks, which may be based on random sampling, in accordance with national law and practice’ (Article 12(4) of the ECI Regulation). In line with the Commission’s guidelines2, several Member States provided the organisers with additional information on the checks carried out and the outcome of the verification.

Causes for invalidation reported included the use of names of legal persons and instances where the names of natural persons were not found in the relevant national registers. Following the verification process, the initiative has not met the conditions for validity in Article 3(1) of the ECI Regulation.
It is only if organisers submit a valid initiative for examination, that the Commission analyses its substance in line with Article 15 of the ECI Regulation.
